personality_voice.book_baseline: In the books, Ron is defined by a distinctive combination of traits: loyal and instinctively protective of Harry, but also quick-tempered, insecure, prone to jealousy, and capable of great emotional immaturity. His voice is characterised by blunt humour, earthy sarcasm, and frequent self-deprecation mixed with moments of genuine sensitivity. He is opinionated (on Quidditch, food, Hermione's causes, Snape's trustworthiness), argumentative, and deeply competitive despite low self-confidence. His speech is direct, often tactless, sometimes clumsy, and laced with colloquial energy. He bristles at being overlooked — whether about his Quidditch failings, Percy's letter, or Hermione copying his work — and his emotional responses are large and unfiltered. He shows real initiative in arguments (the brain room, Percy's letter, the Sirius situation), real fear (spiders, the Quidditch crowd singing, Ron's parents dying in Mrs. Weasley's boggart), and real humour that is organic to his personality rather than performed for others.
personality_voice.film_portrayal: The film preserves Ron's core personality markers: he is visibly warm and loyal toward Harry, instinctively funny in short exchanges, and willing to stand up for Harry against Seamus. His voice retains some of the book's bluntness — 'Not bloody likely' (about the Forbidden Forest), 'Who are you and what have you done with Hermione Granger?', 'Combat? What does he think, we're forming some sort of wizard army?' These lines are recognisably Ron. He is present in most key scenes, reacts in broadly correct emotional registers, and his sarcasm and occasional cluelessness are intact.
personality_voice.difference: However, substantial simplification has occurred. The film Ron is considerably flatter in emotional texture. His insecurity — one of his most defining book traits, explored at length through the Quidditch subplot, the prefect badge episode, and the Percy letter — is reduced to brief reactive shots. His jealousy and complexity with Hermione (the Viktor Krum subplot, the 'you're honestly the most wonderful person I've ever met' payoff, the running arguments) are compressed to near-invisibility. His voice becomes less distinctly his own: many of his best book lines — the extended conversation about career ambitions, the nuanced back-and-forth about Dumbledore's trust in Snape, the private bedroom conversation about Voldemort's weapon — are either absent or collapsed. In the film, Ron's most emotionally complex scenes (reacting to Percy's letter, the Quidditch Keeper arc, the boggart-as-Ron's-corpse moment which never appears) are largely absent. His jealousy toward Krum is reduced to a single clipped exchange. His comic voice is present but thinned: many of his funniest and most characteristic lines (the Goyle/lines impression, the 'one person can't feel all that at once' Cho speech, the spattergroit portrait scene at St. Mungo's) are absent. His speech pattern in the film is more reactive than generative — he responds to others rather than driving exchanges with his own idiosyncratic voice. The film retains the broad outline but loses the textural richness.
personality_voice.penalty_logic: Main personality is preserved — loyalty, humour, bluntness — but multiple secondary and tertiary traits are simplified or removed. Ron's insecurity, competitive spirit, jealousy, and argumentativeness are all present but substantially reduced. His voice is recognisable but thinner and less idiosyncratic. Score lands in the 14–17 range: character remains recognisable but important traits, tone, and contradictions are reduced.

narrative_role_agency.book_baseline: In the books, Ron performs a wide range of active narrative functions. He defends Harry against Seamus (directly, forcefully, using prefect authority). He initiates conversations that drive plot understanding (the weapon in the Department of Mysteries, Sturgis Podmore's arrest, what Voldemort wants). He acts as Harry's sounding board in ways that advance Harry's thinking, not merely reflect it. He performs practical acts of agency: covering his eyes to listen for footsteps at Grimmauld Place, suggesting 'Zacharias Smith!' as the informer, pulling Harry back from the Malfoy confrontation, operating the DA coin system, standing firm in Umbridge's office. In the Department of Mysteries he independently engages with the brain tank (in a misguided but character-defining way), and in the escape sequences he is an active participant. In the Quidditch subplot he is the central figure around whom tension and narrative momentum revolve. He helps organise the DA's first meeting logistics. He keeps watch for Kreacher. He proposes poisoning Umbridge (darkly comic but still agentic). He is a structural support pillar of the narrative's daily texture.
narrative_role_agency.film_portrayal: The film preserves some agency: Ron stands up to Seamus, explicitly backs Harry ('Yeah, I do'), volunteers to distract Umbridge ('I'll do it — I'll tell her Peeves is smashing up the Transfiguration department'), and fights in the Department of Mysteries. He encourages Harry about the DA idea. He participates in most of the key scenes and is physically present throughout. His line 'Maybe you don't have to do this all by yourself, mate' restores a measure of emotional agency near the end.
narrative_role_agency.difference: However, significant agency is transferred or removed. In the film, the Quidditch Keeper arc — in which Ron is the sustained narrative centre across multiple chapters — is almost entirely absent from the corpus. His practical night-by-night role at Grimmauld Place (listening at doors, managing Kreacher, organising logistics) is reduced. His role in the Ministry sequence is diminished: the film gives him a brief comic turn with the brains and shows him incapacitated quickly, but the book's extended sequence where Ron fights on while drugged, helps Neville, and remains a meaningful combatant is condensed. Several scenes where Ron provides plot information to Harry and Hermione (Sturgis Podmore, the Department of Mysteries weapon theory, Voldemort's happiness after the Azkaban breakout) are absent or given more to Hermione. The Percy letter scene — where Ron is the emotional and narrative pivot — is absent from the film corpus. His prefect role, which gives him new agency in the books (confronting Seamus, managing corridors, defending his authority), appears in the film only briefly and without the sustained texture the books provide.
narrative_role_agency.penalty_logic: Role is reduced but recognisable. Several specific acts of agency are transferred to Hermione or removed. Ron functions as a reliable secondary participant but loses the narrative centrality he holds in several book arcs. Score falls in the 10–13 range: role or agency are clearly altered.

motivations_internal_conflict.book_baseline: Ron's motivations in OotP are layered. He genuinely wants to support Harry but also wants to be seen and valued in his own right — the prefect badge, the Keeper tryout, and his reaction to Fred and George's mockery all reveal a young man struggling with the shadow cast by his more famous friends and more accomplished brothers. He fears being inadequate (Quidditch, academics) and fears being disloyal (the Percy letter decision). He has a specific internal conflict about family loyalty: he is hurt and angry about Percy but also embarrassed and sad, as evidenced by his quiet, almost dissociated reaction to telling Harry about the family rupture. He is motivated by affection for Hermione but confused by jealousy about Krum, a conflict he handles with sarcasm rather than directness. He supports Harry's instincts over Hermione's caution at several points, driven by loyalty and a pragmatic rather than rule-based moral compass.
motivations_internal_conflict.film_portrayal: The film establishes Ron's loyalty to Harry as his primary motivation, and this is consistent with the books. His line about going with Harry ('Are you mental? We're going with you') reflects genuine, motivated loyalty. He supports the DA enthusiastically. His concern about Harry's scar and Voldemort's connection is clearly motivated by protectiveness. His 'I'm here for you, mate' (after Seamus confrontation) and his participation in the Ministry mission are coherent expressions of his book motivations.
motivations_internal_conflict.difference: However, the motivations surrounding Ron's personal insecurity, his desire to be valued on his own terms, and his internal conflict about adequacy are largely absent. The Quidditch Keeper arc — which is the primary vehicle in the books for Ron's internal conflict between self-belief and self-doubt — is present only as a background reference without emotional development. His conflict about family loyalty (Percy) is entirely absent. His complicated feelings about Hermione and Krum are reduced to a single brief exchange. The internal conflict about whether to obey Dumbledore's instructions (via Mrs. Weasley's message through Sirius) is simplified. While the core motivations of loyalty survive, the secondary and conflicted motivations are largely flattened.
motivations_internal_conflict.penalty_logic: Motivations are partially altered and significantly underexplained. The core loyalty motivation is intact but Ron's motivations related to self-worth, family loyalty, and his competing desires are mostly missing. Score falls in the 8–10 range.

character_arc.book_baseline: Ron's arc in OotP has two distinct but connected threads. First, a public arc: he begins as Harry's reliable best friend who is overlooked and underestimated (by Fred and George, by Hermione's initial surprise at his prefect badge, by his own self-doubt), works through humiliating failure as Keeper under Slytherin psychological attack, and ultimately triumphs — winning the Quidditch Cup and proving himself capable. This arc is explicitly tied to the book's themes of confidence, self-belief under pressure, and the difficulty of establishing identity when surrounded by exceptional people. Second, a quieter arc: Ron navigates a family crisis (Percy's defection), demonstrates emotional maturity in how he handles it (tearing up Percy's letter without extended breakdown, maintaining loyalty to his family even under pressure), and ends the year having survived genuine danger and loss alongside Harry. By the end, Ron has grown in both competence and quiet resilience.
character_arc.film_portrayal: The film preserves a sketch of Ron's arc: he is seen trying to produce a Patronus (one successful attempt is shown), he participates in DA training, and he fights in the Department of Mysteries. His supportive presence throughout suggests a character who matures alongside Harry. His line near the end ('Maybe you don't have to do this all by yourself, mate') suggests growth toward emotional directness.
character_arc.difference: The Quidditch arc — the primary external arc of the book — is almost entirely absent from the film corpus. The crucial trajectory from humiliating failure to triumphant cup victory (with all its intermediate steps: the crowd chanting, Ron's self-doubt, the first match catastrophe, the final redemption) is not present. The internal arc of growing self-belief under sustained external pressure is therefore missing. The Percy arc, which forms the emotional backbone of Ron's family arc, is absent. The prefect badge subplot — Ron's first moment of being chosen for something independently of Harry — is absent. The film gives Ron no real turning points and no visible progression; he enters and exits the story in essentially the same condition. What arc exists is implied by background participation rather than shown through dramatic development.
character_arc.penalty_logic: The arc is incomplete and missing important steps. The film preserves Ron's general character disposition but removes the specific turning points and developmental beats that constitute his actual arc. Score falls in the 8–10 range: arc is incomplete, rushed, or missing important steps.

key_relationships.book_baseline: Ron's most important relationships in OotP are: (1) Harry — characterised by reciprocal loyalty, occasional tension (Ron's brief hurt at Harry's outbursts, Harry's moment of considering withholding the Order information from Ron), and the specific dynamic of Ron as Harry's emotional anchor and day-to-day companion; (2) Hermione — characterised by bickering, mutual respect, growing romantic tension, jealousy about Krum, and a pattern where Ron's instincts and Hermione's intellect complement and clash; (3) his family — particularly Mrs. Weasley's anxious protectiveness, Percy's betrayal creating a quiet wound, Fred and George's mockery of his prefect status, and Ginny's growing independence; (4) Sirius — Ron treats Sirius with affectionate respect and is genuinely concerned about his isolation at Grimmauld Place.
key_relationships.film_portrayal: The Harry-Ron relationship is mostly preserved in its warmth and basic loyalty. Ron defends Harry, stands by him in the Ministry, and expresses concern. The Hermione-Ron relationship retains its bickering texture in several scenes and the brief Krum jealousy exchange. The family relationships are present in fragments: Mrs. Weasley's protectiveness, Fred and George's energy around Ron.
key_relationships.difference: The Harry-Ron relationship loses the private bedroom conversations, the night-time confidences about Voldemort's moods, and the quieter moments of reciprocal support that give it depth in the books. The specific tension of Ron being excluded from Order information and his complex feelings about that is absent. The Hermione-Ron relationship is substantially compressed: the Krum subplot (which drives real jealousy and tension across multiple chapters) is reduced to one brief exchange; the running arguments about SPEW, Hermione's hats, and her academic standards are absent; the moment where Ron genuinely thanks Hermione ('the most wonderful person I've ever met') exists in the film but is delivered as a throwaway rather than as a culmination of an ongoing dynamic. The Percy relationship — one of the most emotionally significant family dynamics in this book — is entirely absent from the film. The Fred and George mockery of Ron's prefect status, which defines a key sibling dynamic, is not depicted.
key_relationships.penalty_logic: Key relationships are mostly faithful in the Harry dynamic, moderately compressed in the Hermione dynamic, and significantly absent in the family dynamics (especially Percy). The emotional weight of the Hermione relationship is reduced. Score falls in the 7–8 range: relationships are mostly faithful with some compression and simplification.

complexity_nuance_lost_material.book_baseline: Ron in OotP is one of the richest characterisations in the series. His complexity lies in the contradiction between his genuine goodness and his capacity for jealousy, self-pity, and emotional immaturity. He is the loyal friend who nevertheless briefly envies Harry (the prefect badge moment, where Harry honestly confronts his own arrogance by remembering Ron deserves recognition too). He is the brave person who is terrified of letting the team down. He handles Percy's betrayal with more dignity than his age suggests. He is the character who sees through Hermione's occasional pomposity while also depending on her entirely for academic survival. He is funny without trying to be — the Goyle imitation, the dream diary joke, the St. Mungo's portrait scene — because his humour emerges from his character rather than from performance. He is the friend Harry never has to explain himself to. His response to the brain tentacles is not just comedic but reveals something about his impulsiveness; his recovery from the Quidditch failure reveals something about his resilience. All of this texture comes from the sustained accumulation of small scenes across hundreds of pages.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.film_portrayal: The film retains Ron's warmth, loyalty, and blunt humour in functional form. He is recognisably Ron Weasley to any viewer. Several of his best comic lines survive. His emotional core — standing by Harry, supporting the DA, fighting in the Ministry — is preserved.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.difference: However, the film loses the sustained texture that makes book-Ron complex rather than merely likeable. The entire Quidditch arc (insecurity, failure, mockery, triumph) is absent. The prefect badge subplot and the specific contradiction of Ron being chosen over Harry is absent. The Percy letter and Ron's dignified, pained response is absent. The Viktor Krum jealousy, which reveals real emotional immaturity alongside genuine feeling, is reduced to nothing. The night-time conversations in the dormitory — where Ron and Harry talk about Voldemort's moods, about the Department of Mysteries weapon, about whether to trust Snape — are absent. The boggart scene (Mrs. Weasley seeing Ron's dead body) which contextualises the family's terror without Ron even being present is unremarkable but contributes to understanding what Ron means to his family. The extended Cho/Hermione discussion where Ron's emotional limitations are both mocked and affectionately accepted is compressed. The spattergroit portrait scene at St. Mungo's is absent. What remains is a loyal, warm, funny sidekick — recognisable but not the full character.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.penalty_logic: Noticeable simplification across multiple dimensions. Important nuances, contradictions, relationship textures, and arc beats are missing. Ron is reduced toward a supporting function: the loyal best friend who provides comic relief and emotional validation. Score falls in the 8–10 range.

Cap 3 (75): Applied — multiple book actions and emotional beats are transferred to or absorbed by Hermione in the film (theorising about Podmore, initiating the DA idea, several instances of plot explanation), and Ron's Quidditch arc agency is entirely removed

The total score of 64 reflects this assessment
key_observations: The film's Ron Weasley is a faithful surface portrait but a substantially simplified character. The warmth, loyalty, and blunt humour that define him most broadly are preserved, and he is never mischaracterised in any scene he inhabits. However, virtually every subplot and arc that gives book-Ron his complexity and dramatic weight has been removed: the Quidditch Keeper arc, the prefect badge episode, Percy's betrayal, the Viktor Krum jealousy, and the extended dormitory conversations. The film retains Ron as a functioning and likeable presence but reduces him from a three-dimensional character with his own insecurities, triumphs, and contradictions to a loyal supporting figure whose primary function is to validate Harry and provide occasional comic relief. The adaptation loss is not distortion — he is never portrayed as something he is not — but compression so severe that the richness of the book character is almost entirely absent from the screen.
